subject: Random Walk Metropolis for general manifolds

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Random Walk Metropolis for general manifolds
parts:
Hi,

This question is a bit theoretical in nature, so forgive me.

I was wondering - does Random Walk Metropolis work as it does in R_n for manifolds? For example, if we had a von Mises distribution on the sphere, does it work? (I am assuming we are able to determine geodesics on the manifold, and use these to generate dependent samples.)

I have been searching for a while, and can't seem to find the answer to this definitively; I see lots of papers on generalising HMC to manifolds, but haven't seen simple Random Walk Metropolis. The reason for considering the latter is that I am looking at solving an (somewhat expensive) integral equation on the surface of the manifold, and I am just not sure how easy it will be to calculate its derivatives in a reasonable amount of time.

Best,

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Walk Metropolis for general manifolds
parts:
Yes. For example, see Byrne and Girolami's paper:

http://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.6064.pdf

The paper doesn't say why, but if you follow the proofs
for Metropolis-Hastings, you'll find they don't reference
the metric, just the probabilities of moving among measurable
sets.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Walk Metropolis for general manifolds
parts:
Firstly, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is defined on manifolds, it does not
have to be “generalized to manifolds”.  It’s geometric by construction.

Metropolis-Hastings works on arbitrary state spaces, and hence is
fine for manifolds.  The problem is trying to construct a proposal
mechanism that stays on the manifold, which is _very_ hard to do
in general.  If you can construct geodesics then you can emulate
Random Walk by choosing a random direction and flowing along
the geodesic for epsilon time, but otherwise you’d need gradient
information to construct a proper path through the manifold.
On May 14, 2016, at 3:31 AM, 'Ben Lambert' via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

Great, thanks very much Bob. Thought that was the case, but wanted to check.

Best,

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Walk Metropolis for general manifolds
parts:
And that's why there are whole branches of literature devoted
to things like "generating random correlation matrices".

Luckily, it's pretty easy for spheres --- probably why they're
always the first example of non-trivial manifolds.

There's a nice duality between generating random X-es, having
constrained variables that are Xs, and writing densities over Xs.
This is how Ben created the LKJ density out of Lewandowski, Kurowicka,
and Joe's method for generating correlation matrices.

Stan lets you do this automatically for simplexes, ordered
vectors, unit vectors (coming in Stan 2.10), correlation matrices,
and covariance matrices, as well as Cholesky factors of correlation
or covariance matrices. It's just a mass of constraining transforms
and Jacobian calculations (all described in the manual chapter on
transforms/constraints).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Walk Metropolis for general manifolds
parts:
The unit vectors for spheres use the overparameterization
plus prior trick (C^{n} embedded in R^{n+1}). Not an isomorphism,
but it should have better locality for things like wrapping
than the R^{n} version.

- Bob
